title: Termites hollow out the eucalyptus trunks that become traditional didgeridoos

cover.alt: Three tall painted didgeridoos standing upright in a museum display, decorated with bands of red, yellow and black and painted figures.

body: The didgeridoo was probably developed by Aboriginal peoples of northern Australia, possibly in Arnhem Land. A traditional one starts as a living eucalyptus tree that termites have attacked, eating out the dead heartwood at its core and leaving a natural tube. Makers read the landscape and the termites’ habits to find such trees, then peel back a little bark and knock on the wood to hear whether it is hollow. A good trunk is felled, cleaned out, stripped of bark and shaped, and the result, anywhere from **1 to 3 m** long, is played with vibrating lips as a continuous drone.

slides.question: Termites eat out the tree’s core. Why don’t they chew right through the outside too?
options: The bark is too hard to bite
They only feed in the dry season
Makers cut the tree down first
slides.explanation: The termites remove only the dead heartwood. The living sapwood around it contains a chemical that repels them, so it stays as the walls of the tube.

steps.label: Knock on the trunk to hear if it’s hollow
Fell it, clean it out, strip the bark
Shape it, maybe add a beeswax mouthpiece

slides.alt: Five didgeridoos laid side by side above a centimetre scale running to 150 cm, three painted in traditional patterns and two in non-traditional styles.
slides.caption: Five modern eucalyptus didgeridoos. A to C are traditional Aboriginal instruments; D and E are not.

slides.heading: Breathing in while blowing out
slides.text: To keep the drone going without a break, players use circular breathing: they breathe in through the nose while squeezing air out with the cheeks. Over the drone they add vocal sounds, many of them imitating Australian animals.

slides.heading: Aboriginal name or not?
slides.explanation: Yiḏaki is the Yolngu name and mako is used in West Arnhem Land. ‘Didgeridoo’ is thought to imitate the sound; it was in print as ‘did-gery-do’ by 1908.
